newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters walk out of UPS contract talks, call strike.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters walk out of UPS contract talks, call strike.

text.p: The International Brotherhood of Teamsters walked out of last-ditch negotiations and said it would strike United Parcel Service -- the nation's largest small package carrier -- at midnight on Sunday.
Teamsters President Ron Carey said contract negotiations had broken down and there was no sense in continuing talks with a federal mediator and company officials.

"We have exhausted every possible approach to solve the problem," Carey told reporters as the union delegation left the talks just after 10 p.m. EDT (0200 GMT), two hours before the midnight deadline (0400 GMT on Monday GMT).
"At this point, it's a waste of time ... What that means is there's a strike at 12:01 a.m. (EDT)," Carey told reporters.
"It's unfortunate, the company has failed to recognise the needs of our members," Carey said, citing disagreements over subcontracting to non-union workers as one big obstacle.

"As a result our membership is prepared and will be prepared as of 12:01 to strike this company," he said. "To stay there any longer would just be repetition. Somebody's got to stand up and say 'Enough is enough.'"

Chief UPS negotiator Dave Murray called the union's decision to abandon the talks "highly irresponsible" and said the union's leadership should let its members review the company's "last, best and final offer," made last week.

UPS, the largest U.S. parcel carrier, handles 12 million packages a day and employs 301,000 people in the United States, 185,000 of whom are represented by the Teamsters, including package sorters, loaders and drivers.
The Independent Pilots Association is backing the strike and said its 2,000 UPS pilots would refuse work in the event of a strike by package handlers and drivers.
Murray said the company would do all it could to ensure that hospital supplies, blood supplies and packages containing other critical supplies reached their destinations.
"We have many contingency plans," he said.
Federal mediator John Calhoun Wells said the strike would affect hundreds of thousands of workers and millions of UPS customers, resulting in a measurable effect on the U.S. economy.

"We didn't succeed, that's deeply disappointing," said Wells, who directs the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. "I'm going to be in touch with both the Teamsters and UPS as we go foward and hopefully we can add value in coming days."
"They were far enough apart so that we were unable to bridge the gap this evening," he said.
UPS Chairman and CEO James Kelly and his negotiating team arrived about an hour before the union to meet with the mediator and consider a new union proposal, but the talks failed to move forward.
UPS spokeswoman Gina Ellrich said the carrier's shipping volume was already down by one million packages from 12 million, forcing it to lay off several thousand workers.
The White House has been keeping close tabs on the negotiations, but spokesman Barry Toiv said President Bill Clinton did not plan to intervene at this time.

"At this time, the administration does not believe that the standard for interviention under the Taft-Hartley Act has been met," Toiv said, referring to a federal law which has not been used for decades.
Carey said the union was particularly concerned about preventing work going to subcontractors rather than union workers, the pension plan, and health and safety issues.
Union spokesman Rand Wilson said the two sides remained "pretty far apart on all the issues", including whether the contract would last for three, four or five years.
UPS said last week that the threat of a strike was costing it about $5 million a day in business lost to competitors such as the Postal Service and Federal Express Corp.

In its contract offer the company offered to boost pay for both full- and part-time workers by $1.50 to $2.50 per hour over five years. Under the company proposal, a profit-sharing plan would provide a first payment of $3,060 to full-time employees and $1,530 to part-time workers in 1997.
With revenue of $22.4 billion in 1996, UPS annually handles about 3 billion parcels and documents, shipped to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
